travel.transfersIntro: If you’re arriving at Mexico City International Airport (MEX / AICM), you can continue directly to Puebla by bus or arrange a private transfer.
travel.busBody: Estrella Roja runs hourly buses from Terminal 1 and Terminal 2 to Puebla. Tickets can be bought on site at the airport bus ticket counters. Check the Puebla drop-off point before arranging the final journey to your hotel. Allow time for immigration, baggage collection and traffic when planning your connection.

zocalo.heading: Welcome to Puebla
zocalo.intro: We recommend everyone stays within a few blocks of the Zócalo, Puebla’s main square, which puts the whole of the Centro Histórico — a UNESCO World Heritage site — within a short walk of your door. Here is what you could do with a free morning or an afternoon between events.

catedral.name: Catedral de Puebla
catedral.blurb: The twin towers are the tallest cathedral towers in Mexico. Step inside for the marble and gilt altar, then — if the bell-tower visit is running, weekends only and tickets at the door — climb it for a view over the tiled domes.

rosario.name: Capilla del Rosario
rosario.blurb: Tucked inside the Templo de Santo Domingo, this gold-leaf baroque chapel was called the eighth wonder of the New World when it opened in 1690. Free to enter, and worth going back to twice.

palafoxiana.name: Biblioteca Palafoxiana
palafoxiana.blurb: The first public library in the Americas, founded in 1646 — 45,000 volumes on tiered cedar shelves, in a hall unchanged since the 1770s. Small entrance fee, closed Mondays.

munecos.name: Casa de los Muñecos
munecos.blurb: The tiled facade on the north-east corner is covered in caricatures of the councillors who tried to stop the owner building higher than they had. He won, and made sure everyone knew.

santaRosa.name: Ex-Convento de Santa Rosa
santaRosa.blurb: The Talavera-tiled convent kitchen where mole poblano was supposedly invented, now the city’s Talavera museum. Go before you eat the mole rather than after.

sapos.name: Callejón de los Sapos
sapos.blurb: Antique shops by day, a flea market on Saturday and Sunday, cantinas with live music after dark. Stop at La Pasita in the afternoon before it shuts: one shot, one cube of cheese, one raisin.

artista.name: Barrio del Artista & El Parián
artista.blurb: Painters keep open studios around a small plaza, and El Parián next door is good for cheerful souvenirs. For certified Talavera, walk five blocks west to Uriarte instead — same workshop since 1824, and you can watch them paint it.

amparo.name: Museo Amparo
amparo.blurb: Pre-Hispanic and colonial collections in a beautifully restored mansion, and a rooftop terrace café with the best view of the cathedral in the city. Closed Tuesdays, not Mondays.

fuertes.name: Fuertes de Loreto y Guadalupe
fuertes.blurb: The hill where the outnumbered Mexican army won on the fifth of May, 1862 — the reason the date means anything at all. Ramparts, a museum, and the long view back over the city.

mole.title: Mole poblano
mole.body: Puebla claims to have invented it, in a convent kitchen. Fonda de Santa Clara on 3 Poniente is the reliable classic and El Mural de los Poetas is where we would go for a proper dinner — have it with turkey, and skip the arcade restaurants on the square itself.

chiles.title: Chiles en nogada
chiles.body: The dish Puebla is most famous for — a stuffed poblano under walnut cream — but it only appears once the nuez de Castilla is harvested, from late July. You will be two months early, so put it on the list for a return trip and eat mole instead.

cemitas.title: Cemitas & tacos árabes
cemitas.body: The city’s two great sandwiches. A cemita is a sesame roll with quesillo, avocado, chipotle and papalo — Mercado El Carmen for the real thing. Tacos árabes come off a vertical spit in pan árabe rather than a tortilla, and are worth staying up for.

dulces.title: Calle de los Dulces
dulces.body: 6 Oriente is lined with sweet shops — camotes, borrachitos and tortitas de Santa Clara, sold from the same doorways since before the revolution.

rooftop.title: Sunset from a rooftop
rooftop.body: The terraces on the square look straight at the cathedral, and on a clear evening Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl sit off to the west, to your right. The end of May is the turn of the rainy season, so the volcanoes show themselves more often in the morning than at dusk. Either way: mezcal, and stay for the light.

cholula.title: Cholula — 20 minutes
cholula.body: The Great Pyramid is the largest by volume in the world, with a yellow church sitting on top of it. Walk the tunnel if it is open, climb up for the volcano view, then have lunch on the plaza below. Closed Mondays.

tonantzintla.title: Tonantzintla & Acatepec — 30 minutes
tonantzintla.body: Two village churches beside Cholula. Acatepec is the Talavera-tiled facade; Tonantzintla is the one to go inside, for a ceiling of indigenous saints, fruit and feathered angels carved by the villagers themselves. No photographs in there.

atlixco.title: Atlixco — 45 minutes
atlixco.body: A flower-growing town with a painted village square and the Cerro de San Miguel viewpoint over the valley. The nurseries are in full colour in late spring, and the drive out is half the pleasure.

mondays.title: A word on Mondays
mondays.body: Almost every museum in Mexico closes on Monday, the Palafoxiana and the Cholula pyramid included. Museo Amparo is the odd one out and closes on Tuesday. Churches are open every day.

altitude.title: 2,135 metres
altitude.body: Puebla sits high. On your first day drink more water than you want to and let the mezcal go slowly — the altitude catches everyone out.

cash.title: Cash & cards
cash.body: Restaurants and hotels take cards; markets, the sweet shops and street taxis want pesos. Draw from a bank ATM and decline the machine’s own exchange rate. Ten to fifteen per cent is the tip.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.body: Uber and DiDi both work well here and cost very little across the Centro. Use them rather than street taxis, use them late at night, and use them to get out to Cholula.

pack.title: What to pack
pack.body: The end of May is warm by day and cool once the sun goes down, and the rains are just beginning — a jacket for the evenings, a light rain layer for the afternoon storms, and flat shoes for the cobbles.

explore.heading: Where to Go in Mexico
explore.intro: You are flying a long way for one weekend — so stay a little longer. These are the four places we would send you, whether you have two extra days or two extra weeks.
explore.outro: And if you would rather not go far: Puebla and the surrounding towns make for great sights and hikes.
explore.tagline: Come for the wedding, stay for the country.

mexicoCity.name: Mexico City
mexicoCity.blurb: If you add only one stop, make it this one: a great museum city wrapped around a colonial centre, with some of the best eating anywhere in the world.
mexicoCity.gettingThere: ADO leaves Puebla’s CAPU terminal every twenty minutes and takes about two hours, arriving at TAPO on the east side. There are direct CAPU buses to the airport too — much better than crossing the city.

highlights.h1: Museo Nacional de Antropología — the finest museum in the country. Give it half a day, then walk up to Chapultepec Castle for the view.
highlights.h2: The Centro Histórico: the Zócalo, Templo Mayor, Bellas Artes, and the Diego Rivera murals in the Palacio Nacional — bring your passport and check it is open.
highlights.h3: Frida Kahlo’s Casa Azul in Coyoacán — timed tickets sell out weeks ahead, so book online before you fly.
highlights.h4: Roma and Condesa for long lunches, tree-lined streets and cocktails afterwards.
highlights.h5: Teotihuacán, an hour north — arrive at opening, or float over the pyramids in a balloon.
highlights.h6: Lucha libre at Arena México on a Friday night — Super Viernes is the big card, and tickets are cheap.

oaxaca.name: Oaxaca City
oaxaca.region: Oaxaca · 4½ hrs by road from Puebla, 1 hr by air from Mexico City
oaxaca.blurb: The country’s food and craft capital — mezcal, seven moles and markets you would fly in for on their own. Two nights minimum, three if you can.
oaxaca.gettingThere: There is no direct flight from Puebla: fly from Mexico City in an hour, take ADO straight from CAPU, or drive the 135D toll road through the mountains in four and a half hours — that one in daylight.

highlights.h1: Mercado 20 de Noviembre for the Pasillo de Humo, the smoke-filled grill hall, with Mercado Benito Juárez next door.
highlights.h2: Santo Domingo and its cultural museum — the ethnobotanical garden is guided-tour only, and English tours run just a few times a week.
highlights.h3: Monte Albán, the Zapotec city on the ridge, thirty minutes above town, with Mitla and the vast tree at El Tule out in the valley.
highlights.h4: The Sunday market at Tlacolula, and the rug weavers and mezcal palenques of Teotitlán del Valle on the way.
highlights.h5: Hierve el Agua’s petrified waterfalls, best as an early start — check it is open first, the community closes the road from time to time.
highlights.h6: Late May and June are the green season: the valleys turn after the first rains and the city is quiet, before the Guelaguetza crowds arrive in July.

puertoEscondido.name: Puerto Escondido
puertoEscondido.region: Oaxacan coast · 1 hr by air from Mexico City
puertoEscondido.blurb: Where Mexico City goes to swim: barefoot, unpolished and warm all year. The easiest possible way to end a trip.
puertoEscondido.gettingThere: An hour from Mexico City by air, or forty minutes from Oaxaca City in a twelve-seat prop plane — pack light, the bag limit is strict. The new highway has cut the drive down from Oaxaca to about three and a half hours.

highlights.h1: Playa Carrizalillo for the calm swimming cove — there are a hundred and seventy steps down to it.
highlights.h2: Zicatela for the surf and the sunset, but do not get in the water there: it is the Mexican Pipeline, the summer swell is already running by June, and the rips are lethal.
highlights.h3: Bioluminescence on the Manialtepec lagoon, best on a moonless night once the rains have started.
highlights.h4: A dawn boat trip for dolphins and turtles — the whales have gone north by June, but the turtles are just beginning to nest.
highlights.h5: Baby-turtle releases at Playa Bacocho, which start up again as the nesting season opens.
highlights.h6: Mazunte and Zipolite, ninety minutes east, if you want somewhere quieter still.

sanMiguel.name: San Miguel de Allende
sanMiguel.region: Guanajuato · 3½ hrs by road from Mexico City
sanMiguel.blurb: Cobblestones, rooftop bars and a pink church out of a fairy tale, in a town small enough to walk end to end. Made for a slow two nights.
sanMiguel.gettingThere: Fly into Querétaro (QRO) and drive an hour, or León (BJX) and drive an hour and three-quarters; comfortable buses also run from Mexico City.

highlights.h1: The Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel on the Jardín — best at golden hour from a rooftop, and the one everyone means is Luna at the Rosewood.
highlights.h2: Fábrica La Aurora, an old textile mill full of galleries and studios.
highlights.h3: Hot springs at La Gruta or Escondido Place, twenty minutes out — cash only, and packed at weekends.
highlights.h4: Atotonilco, the frescoed sanctuary fifteen minutes away, and the cactus gardens at El Charco del Ingenio.
highlights.h5: The Tuesday tianguis out on the Querétaro road — huge, cheap and not walkable, so take a taxi.
highlights.h6: Guanajuato city, ninety minutes away, for tunnels, callejones and colour.
